title: Mass Atrocities and Causation in Global Conflict
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: In 1944, the Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word 'genocide' by combining the Greek 'genos' (people or race) with the Latin 'cide' (killing), to describe the deliberate, organized attempt to destroy an entire people. In 1948 the United Nations made genocide a crime under international law.

The Armenian Genocide began in 1915 within the collapsing Ottoman Empire during World War I. Gripped by an ultranationalist 'Turkification' ideology, the Ottoman government treated the Christian Armenian minority as an internal enemy and carried out deportations and killings that took an estimated one million or more lives.

The Armenian Genocide is widely regarded as the first modern, systematically organized genocide of the twentieth century, foreshadowing later atrocities in its use of state organization, wartime cover, and an ideology defining a minority as a dangerous enemy.

The Holocaust (roughly 1941–1945) was Nazi Germany's deliberate, bureaucratically organized, industrialized extermination of six million European Jews, along with millions of Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, political dissidents, and others.

The Nazis moved from persecution and ghettos to mass shootings by mobile killing squads and finally to purpose-built death camps using poison gas, turning industry, bureaucracy, and the railroad toward the assembly-line murder of human beings.

Other atrocities of the era included Stalin's forced collectivization and famines (such as the Ukrainian famine) and the Great Purges, Imperial Japan's atrocities across Asia including the Rape of Nanjing, and the deliberate bombing of civilian cities culminating in the atomic bombings.

Despite different settings, the great atrocities of the era share features: they were state-organized efforts to destroy or devastate a targeted group, carried out under the cover of war by ultranationalist or totalitarian regimes that dehumanized their victims and used modern means.

The context of war is a key enabling cause of mass atrocity: war creates emergency conditions, suspends normal moral and legal limits, hardens the line between 'us' and the enemy, and provides both chaos and concealment. Both the Armenian Genocide and the Holocaust occurred during world wars.

Genocide on a mass scale requires a powerful totalitarian or authoritarian state with the bureaucratic reach to identify, round up, transport, and kill huge numbers of people, and the concentrated, unchecked power to override any opposition.

A scapegoating ideology — an ultranationalist or racist worldview that defines a minority as an alien, dangerous internal enemy responsible for the nation's problems — is a core cause of genocide. Nazi antisemitism and Ottoman 'Turkification' both did this work.

The scapegoating ideologies behind twentieth-century genocide connect back to the scientific racism and social Darwinism of the age of imperialism, which had taught societies to rank human groups as superior and inferior.
Dehumanization — systematic propaganda that strips the targeted group of their humanity — is a cause of atrocity because it makes ordinary people willing to participate in or tolerate mass murder.

Modern technology and organization — railroads, bureaucracies, communications, and industrial methods — are a distinctive cause of twentieth-century genocide, allowing killing to be organized systematically and on an unprecedented, assembly-line scale.

No single factor is sufficient to cause genocide; it is the combination — war plus a powerful state plus a scapegoating ideology plus dehumanization plus modern technology — that is so lethal. Analyzing causation means identifying interacting conditions, not a single villain.

Strong causation analysis distinguishes long-term causes (such as racist and nationalist ideologies built up over decades) from immediate causes (such as the outbreak of war or a regime's decision) and explains how the two interact to produce an outcome.

A strong causation LEQ thesis takes a defensible, specific, arguable position that prioritizes among causes — for example, that ideology created the potential for genocide but total war and totalitarian state power turned that potential into systematic mass murder — rather than vaguely stating 'there were many causes.'

Contextualization earns its own point on the LEQ: a sentence or two of broader context, such as the nineteenth-century rise of scientific racism and aggressive nationalism or the collapse of multi-ethnic empires in WWI, situates the argument in the bigger picture.

Causation essays require specific, accurate evidence, not generic claims: for example, that the Nazi regime used railroads and purpose-built death camps to murder six million Jews, or that the Ottoman government deported and killed over a million Armenians in 1915.

The complexity point rewards nuance: acknowledging that many states held racist ideologies and fought wars without committing genocide shows that no single cause was sufficient, and that the specific combination of conditions was decisive — sophisticated necessary-but-not-sufficient reasoning.

Common causation-essay pitfalls penalized by AP readers include vague theses, generic evidence, listing causes without analyzing how they connect to the outcome, using evidence outside the prompt's time period, and confusing correlation with causation.

The reusable causation toolkit: distinguish long-term from immediate causes, sort causes into categories (political, economic, social, cultural, ideological), weigh which mattered most, show how causes interact, and for complexity note necessary-but-not-sufficient causes or connect across regions and time.

The framework identifying the conditions that make genocide possible is the same framework scholars, human-rights organizations, and the United Nations use to recognize warning signs and try to prevent atrocities, showing why analyzing interacting causes matters beyond the exam.
